Title: Website Development: HTML → CSS → JavaScript — Sign-In Project

Contents.Title: Introduction!
Contents.Contents:
Welcome!

Welcome to Website Development. This course is designed for someone who may have never programmed before, so we will begin with the smallest ideas and build them into a complete interface.

We are going to learn three main technologies:

  • HTML creates the structure of the webpage.
  • CSS creates the visual design.
  • JavaScript creates behavior and interaction.

We will not throw all three at you at once. We will learn them in that order so you can understand what each one is responsible for.

Our First Goal

Our first project is a Sign-In interface. Later, the project will grow into a Sign-Up system and eventually a POS application. For now, we are only learning the foundation.

You do not need to memorize everything. Understand what each piece does, why we use it, and what changes when you edit it.

Contents.Title: HTML: What Is HTML?
Contents.Contents:
What Is HTML?

HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language.

HTML describes the structure and meaning of content on a webpage. It tells the browser that something is a heading, paragraph, form, input, button, table, section, and so on.

<h1>Welcome Back</h1>
<p>Login to continue</p>
<button>Login</button>

The browser reads the tags and creates those elements.

HTML Is the Structure

Imagine a house. Before the colors, furniture, and decorations are added, the building still needs walls, rooms, doors, and floors. HTML plays a similar role for a webpage.

CSS will later control the appearance, and JavaScript will later control the behavior.

Contents.Title: The Basic HTML Document
Contents.Contents:
Every Page Needs a Starting Structure

Before adding visible content, create the basic HTML document.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
</head>
<body>
</body>
</html>

<!DOCTYPE html>

This tells the browser that the document should be interpreted using modern HTML rules.

<html>

This is the root element. The whole webpage is placed inside it.

<head>

The <head> contains information about the webpage that helps the browser understand and configure the page. We will learn what belongs inside the head in the next lesson.

<body>

The <body> contains the actual webpage content that belongs to the user interface, such as headings, paragraphs, images, forms, buttons, and other visible elements.

Try It

Now build the complete basic HTML document in the editor. Make sure your document contains <!DOCTYPE html>, the root <html> element, a <head>, and a <body>.

After running it, add a simple heading inside <body> and run it again. Observe that the content inside the <body> becomes visible on the webpage, while the <head> is used for information about the document.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Hello World</h1>
</body>
</html>

Keep using the same project you have been building. Do not start over with unrelated code. The goal is to understand how the basic parts of an HTML document fit together.

Contents.Title: The Head: Page Information
Contents.Contents:
What Goes Inside <head>?

<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>My First Website</title>
</head>

charset

charset="UTF-8" tells the browser which character encoding is being used. UTF-8 supports a very large range of characters and symbols. You can skip this part!

viewport

The viewport setting is especially important for mobile devices. It tells the browser to use the device's actual viewport width when displaying the page.

title

The title element gives the webpage its browser title.

Try It

Now try the change from this lesson in the editor. Continue using the same project you have been building instead of starting over with unrelated code.

Contents.Title: Start With a div
Contents.Contents:
First, We Need a Container

Our webpage will eventually contain many related elements. The first thing we can add is a <div>.

<body>
  <div>
  </div>
</body>

A div is a general-purpose container. It does not mean "login" or "card" or "button." It simply gives us a box in the document that can contain other elements.

Think of it as an empty container or panel. We can put the parts of our interface inside it and later use CSS or JavaScript to work with the group.

Why Start With a Container?

Large interfaces are easier to build when related pieces are grouped. We are going to place our first Sign-In content inside this container.

Try It

Now try the change from this lesson in the editor. Continue using the same project you have been building instead of starting over with unrelated code.

Contents.Title: Add a Heading
Contents.Contents:
Now Add the Main Heading

After creating our container, we can place a heading inside it.

<div>
  <h1>Welcome Back</h1>
</div>

The <h1> represents the main heading.

Notice the order: first we created the container, then we placed the heading inside it. This is called nesting.

The h1 element already tells us what this content is.

Try It

Now try the change from this lesson in the editor. Continue using the same project you have been building instead of starting over with unrelated code.

Contents.Title: Add a Paragraph
Contents.Contents:
After the Heading, Add an Explanation

Our heading tells the user where they are. Now we can add a short explanation.

<div>
  <h1>Welcome Back</h1>
  <p>Login to continue</p>
</div>

The <p> element represents a paragraph.

Again, we do not need a class or ID. We are only describing the content.

Try It

Now try the change from this lesson in the editor. Continue using the same project you have been building instead of starting over with unrelated code.

Contents.Title: Create the Form
Contents.Contents:
Now Add the Form

A Sign-In interface needs a place for the user to enter information. HTML provides the <form> element for this.

<div>
  <h1>Welcome Back</h1>
  <p>Login to continue</p>

  <form>
  </form>
</div>

The form groups controls that belong to the same input process.

We are building from outside to inside: the container contains the heading, paragraph, and form.

Try It

Now try the change from this lesson in the editor. Continue using the same project you have been building instead of starting over with unrelated code.

Contents.Title: Add a Label
Contents.Contents:
Tell the User What the Input Is For

Inside the form, our first field needs a label.

<form>
  <label>Email</label>
</form>

The <label> element tells the user what a control is asking for.

Right now the label is just text. Soon we will connect it to the exact input it describes. We will only introduce the extra attributes when we actually need them.

Try It

Now try the change from this lesson in the editor. Continue using the same project you have been building instead of starting over with unrelated code.

Contents.Title: Add an Input
Contents.Contents:
Now Let the User Enter Something

After creating the label, we need something that allows the user to actually enter information.

<form>
  <label>Email</label>
  <input>
</form>

<input>

The <input> element creates an interactive control where the user can enter or select information.

Why Doesn't <input> Have a Closing Tag?

You may notice something strange: we wrote <input>, but there is no </input>.

This is because <input> is a void element. A void element cannot contain other HTML content, so HTML does not use a separate closing tag for it.

Compare it with the <label> element:

<label>Email</label>

The label has content inside it, so it needs both an opening tag and a closing tag.

The input does not contain content between two tags. The input itself represents the control:

<input>

There is therefore no </input> tag.

Void Elements

<input> is one example of a void element. Other common void elements include <br>, <hr>, <img>, <meta>, and <link>.

They are written without a separate closing tag because they do not wrap content.

Try It

Now add an <input> to the form you have been building. Notice that it does not need a closing </input> tag. Run the page and observe the input control that the browser creates.

<form>
  <label>Email</label>
  <input>
</form>

Keep using the same project you have been building. Do not start over with unrelated code. The goal is to understand how an input element works and why its structure is different from elements that have both an opening and closing tag.

Contents.Title: The type Attribute
Contents.Contents:
Tell the Input What Kind of Data It Accepts

The type attribute changes the purpose of an input.

<input type="text">
<input type="email">
<input type="password">
<input type="number">

text

A normal text field.

email

A field intended for an email address. The browser can use this information for appropriate input behavior and validation.

password

A password field where the entered characters are normally hidden.

number

A field intended for numeric input.

The important idea is that input creates the control, while the type attribute describes what kind of control it should be.

Try It

Now try the change from this lesson in the editor. Continue using the same project you have been building instead of starting over with unrelated code.

Contents.Title: Useful Input Attributes
Contents.Contents:
Give the Input More Information

Now we can make the email input more useful.

<input
  type="email"
  placeholder="you@example.com"
  required
>

placeholder

placeholder displays a temporary hint inside the input. It can show an example of what the user should enter.

required

required tells the browser that the user should not leave the field empty when the form is submitted.

The placeholder is only a hint. It is not a replacement for the label.

Try It

Now try the change from this lesson in the editor. Continue using the same project you have been building instead of starting over with unrelated code.

Contents.Title: Connect the Label With for + id
Contents.Contents:
Now We Have a Reason to Use id

We have a label and an input, but the label is not explicitly connected to that input yet.

HTML gives us two attributes for this: the label's for attribute and the input's id attribute.

<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email">

The label's for value matches the input's id value.

for="email"
     ↓
id="email"

Why This Is Important

Now the browser knows that the label belongs to that particular input. This is a real reason to use an ID, so this is the point where we introduce it.

We do not give every element an ID simply because we can. Add one when you actually need a unique identity.

Try It

Now try the change from this lesson in the editor. Continue using the same project you have been building instead of starting over with unrelated code.

Contents.Title: Add the Password Field
Contents.Contents:
Build the Second Field

We can use the same pattern for the password.

<label for="password">Password</label>
<input
  id="password"
  type="password"
  placeholder="Enter password"
  required
>

Now the password label points to the password input, just as the email label points to the email input.

Try It

Now try the change from this lesson in the editor. Continue using the same project you have been building instead of starting over with unrelated code.

Contents.Title: Add the Login Button
Contents.Contents:
Finish the Basic Form

The user needs a control that submits the form.

<button type="submit">Login</button>

<button> creates the clickable control.

type="submit" tells the browser that this button is intended to submit the form.

At this point, we have the basic HTML structure of a Sign-In interface.

Try It
