Contents.Title: More Useful HTML Tags
Contents.Contents:
Other Tags You Will Use Later

Before moving into CSS, there are a few useful HTML elements worth recognizing.

<strong>

Marks text as important.

<em>

Marks text as emphasized.

<section>

Represents a meaningful section of related content.

<textarea>

Creates a multi-line text input.

<ul>, <ol>, and <li>

Create unordered lists, ordered lists, and list items.

<table>, <tr>, <th>, and <td>

Build tables containing rows, headings, and data cells. These will become useful later when we build a POS order table.

Contents.Title: HTML: class Comes When We Have a Reason
Contents.Contents:
We Are About to Start Styling

Before CSS, there is one more attribute that becomes very useful: class.

A class gives an element a reusable name.

<div class="form-group">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" type="email">
</div>

We can use the same class on several related elements.

<div class="form-group">...</div>
<div class="form-group">...</div>

Why are we adding it now? Because we are about to teach CSS, and CSS needs a reusable way to select groups of elements.

Try It

Now try the change from this lesson in the editor. Continue using the same project you have been building instead of starting over with unrelated code.

Contents.Title: Add the Sign-Up Structure
Contents.Contents:
Our Project Will Have Login and Sign Up

The HTML fundamentals are enough to create the second form as well. We will place it inside the same authentication card.

<div>
  <h1>Create Account</h1>
  <p>Create an account</p>

  <form>

    <div class="form-group">
      <label>Name</label>
      <input type="text" placeholder="Your name" required>
    </div>

    <div class="form-group">
      <label>Email</label>
      <input type="email" placeholder="you@example.com" required>
    </div>

    <div class="form-group">
      <label>Password</label>
      <input type="password" minlength="6" required>
    </div>

    <div class="form-group">
      <label>Confirm Password</label>
      <input type="password" required>
    </div>

    <button type="submit">Sign Up</button>

  </form>
</div>

Notice how the same HTML concepts keep returning. That repetition is intentional. We are learning the concepts and then using them in a real interface.

Try It

Add the Sign-Up structure below or beside your Login structure and observe how the document grows.

Contents.Title: Complete Our HTML Structure Before Styling
Contents.Contents:
Put the HTML Pieces Together

We have learned the individual HTML pieces. Now we will combine them into the structure that CSS is going to style.

<div class="auth-overlay">

  <section class="auth-card">

    <div>
      <h1>Welcome Back</h1>
      <p>Login to continue</p>

      <form>

        <div class="form-group">
          <label for="email">Email</label>
          <input
            id="email"
            type="email"
            placeholder="you@example.com"
            required
          >
        </div>

        <div class="form-group">
          <label for="password">Password</label>
          <input
            id="password"
            type="password"
            placeholder="Enter password"
            required
          >
        </div>

        <button type="submit">Login</button>

      </form>
    </div>

  </section>

</div>

Notice What We Did

We did not add classes and IDs everywhere. The classes exist because CSS will need to style groups such as the card and form groups. The IDs exist where elements need a unique identity, such as connecting a label to an input.

This is the structure we will keep building and styling. We are not starting a new project for CSS.

Try It

Put this structure into the editor and make sure you understand which element is inside which container before moving on.

Contents.Title: CSS: What Is CSS?
Contents.Contents:
Now We Need Styling

HTML created the structure. CSS is the language we use to control how that structure looks.

With CSS we can control colors, spacing, sizes, alignment, borders, shadows, fonts, responsive layout, and many other visual properties.

body {
  background: #0f1115;
  color: white;
}

Here, body is the thing we want to style, background is the property, and #0f1115 is the value.

Contents.Title: CSS: Three Ways to Add Styling
Contents.Contents:
How Can CSS Be Added?

CSS can be added to HTML in three common ways.

1. Inline style attribute

<p style="color:red;">Hello</p>

The style attribute puts CSS directly on one HTML element. It is useful for very specific situations, but large interfaces can become difficult to maintain if every element has its own inline styles.

2. The <style> Tag

<style>
  p {
    color: red;
  }
</style>

This keeps CSS inside the HTML document. For this course, this is the method we will use while learning because you can clearly see the structure and the styling in one place.

3. An External CSS File

<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">

This places CSS in a separate file. It is excellent for larger projects and is often how real projects organize their styles.

Contents.Title: CSS: Add the style Tag
Contents.Contents:
Now Add the <style> Tag

We chose the style-tag method for this course.

We can place the <style> tag inside the HTML document. Most commonly, we put it in the <head> because it contains styling rules for the page.

<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1.0">
  <title>Sign In</title>

  <style>

  </style>
</head>

Now the HTML has a place where our CSS rules can live.

Try It

Now continue with the code you have built so far. Make one small change, run it, and observe what happens before continuing to the next lesson.

Contents.Title: CSS: How Do We Tell CSS Which Element to Style?
Contents.Contents:
Selectors

We have our style tag, but CSS still needs to know which elements the rules should affect.

That is the job of a selector.

body {
  background: #0f1115;
}

The selector is body.

It means: find the <body> element and apply these rules to it.

Inside the braces, we write properties and their values.

selector {
  property: value;
}

Element selectors such as body, h1, and button select elements by their tag name.

Try It

Now try the change from this lesson in the editor. Continue using the same project you have been building instead of starting over with unrelated code.

Contents.Title: CSS: Select the Class We Just Added
Contents.Contents:
Now Use the class We Added

Earlier, we added class="form-group" because we knew we would need to style the repeated field groups.

In CSS, we select a class by writing a dot first, followed by the class name.

.form-group {
  margin-bottom: 15px;
}

The dot . means "this is a class selector."

So .form-group means:

Select every element whose class includes "form-group".

This is why classes are reusable. One CSS rule can style all of the form groups.

Another Example

.auth-card {
  padding: 28px;
}

The browser finds the element with the auth-card class and applies the padding rule.

Try It

Now continue with the code you have built so far. Make one small change, run it, and observe what happens before continuing to the next lesson.

Contents.Title: CSS: Build the Page Background
Contents.Contents:
Start With the Page

Before we design the Sign-In card itself, we should first decide what the entire webpage should look like.

Right now, the browser is using its own default appearance. The page may have a white background, default spacing around the content, and a default font. That is useful for learning HTML, but we now want to take control of the appearance ourselves.

To do that, we write CSS rules for the <body> element.

body {
  margin: 0;
  min-height: 100vh;
  background: #0f1115;
  color: #e8eaf0;
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
}

First: What Does body Mean Here?

You may notice that we are writing body instead of something beginning with a dot.

In CSS, the word before the opening brace is called the selector. A selector tells CSS which HTML elements should receive the styles.

Because body is an HTML tag name, this selector means: find the page's body element and apply these rules to it.

Everything we see on the webpage normally exists somewhere inside the body, so styling the body is a convenient way to establish the page's basic appearance.

margin: 0

Let's begin with margin.

Margin is the space outside an element. Browsers apply some default margin to certain elements, including the body. If we do nothing, our webpage can start with unexpected space around the edges.

We write:

margin: 0;

The value 0 means that the margin should be zero.

Why not leave it blank? Because we want to decide the spacing ourselves. Removing the default body margin gives us a predictable starting point.

Can margin Have Other Values?

Yes. For example:

margin: 20px;

means 20 pixels of space around the element.

You can also write different values for different sides:

margin-top: 20px;
margin-right: 10px;
margin-bottom: 30px;
margin-left: 5px;

You can also use shorthand:

margin: 20px 10px 30px 5px;

The four values represent top, right, bottom, left, in that order.

We are using margin: 0 here because the page itself should start without the browser's default outer gap.

min-height: 100vh

Next we need to understand min-height.

height controls how tall an element should be. min-height is slightly different: it says the element should be at least this tall, but it is allowed to become taller if its content requires more space.

We use:

min-height: 100vh;

Now we have another new unit: vh.

vh means viewport height. The viewport is the visible area of the browser window or device screen.

100vh means 100 percent of the viewport height.

So:

min-height: 100vh;

basically says: make the body at least as tall as the visible screen.

Could We Use Other Values?

Yes. You could write:

min-height: 50vh;

which means at least half of the viewport height.

You could also use fixed units:

min-height: 500px;

or other CSS length units.

We choose 100vh because our Sign-In interface will eventually be centered within the visible screen.

background: #0f1115

Now we need to decide what the page should look like behind our Sign-In card.

The background property controls the background of the element.

background: #0f1115;

The value #0f1115 is a hexadecimal color.

What Does #0f1115 Mean?

A hexadecimal color uses six hexadecimal digits to describe red, green, and blue values.

#RRGGBB

The first two characters represent red, the middle two represent green, and the last two represent blue.

So #0f1115 is a very dark color with small amounts of red, green, and blue.

Can background Have Other Values?

Absolutely. You could write a named color:

background: black;

A hexadecimal color:

background: #222222;

An RGB color:

background: rgb(15, 17, 21);

Or even a gradient:

background: linear-gradient(#111, #222);

For our project, we use a solid dark color because we want a simple, clean foundation for the Sign-In interface.

color: #e8eaf0

Now we need to think about the text.

The color property controls the foreground text color of an element.

color: #e8eaf0;

This is a light color, so normal text can be seen against our dark background.

Notice that background and color are different properties.

background = what is behind the content
color = the text's foreground color

If we changed the background to black while keeping a very dark text color, the text could become difficult to read. Good design requires enough contrast between the foreground and background.

font-family: system-ui, sans-serif

Now we decide which font the page should use.

The font-family property tells the browser which font family should be used for text.

font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;

There are actually two values here: system-ui and sans-serif.

They form a font stack.

The browser first tries to use system-ui, which generally means the interface font used by the user's operating system. If that choice cannot be used, the browser can move to the next option, sans-serif.

What Is sans-serif?

A sans-serif font is a font without the small decorative strokes known as serifs. Examples include common interface fonts used by operating systems and browsers.

You could also specify a particular font family, such as:

font-family: Arial, sans-serif;

The second value is still a fallback. This is important because the exact same font may not exist on every device.

Putting the Whole Rule Together

Now you can understand the entire block instead of memorizing it as one mysterious piece of code:

body {
  margin: 0;
  min-height: 100vh;
  background: #0f1115;
  color: #e8eaf0;
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
}

We removed unwanted outer spacing, made the page at least screen-height, created a dark background, chose a readable text color, and selected a font.

Practice the Complete Rule

Now reproduce the complete CSS rule in the editor. Then experiment with the values one at a time. Change margin: 0 to margin: 30px and observe the gap around the page. Change min-height: 100vh to 50vh and observe the change in page height. Change the hexadecimal background color to another color and see how it affects the page. Finally, change font-family to another available font stack and observe the difference in the text.

Contents.Title: CSS: Center the Authentication Overlay
Contents.Contents:
Now We Need to Position Our Sign-In Interface

We have given the whole page a background, but our Sign-In content still needs to be positioned properly.

Our goal is simple: we want the authentication area to cover the available screen and place the Sign-In card in the center.

Earlier we created a class for the outer container:

<div class="auth-overlay">
  ...
</div>

Because this is a class, we select it in CSS using a dot:

.auth-overlay {

The dot means we are selecting the class named auth-overlay.

position: fixed

The first property is position.

The position property changes how an element participates in page positioning.

Here we use:

position: fixed;

fixed is one possible value of the position property.

It tells the browser that the element should be positioned relative to the viewport rather than simply flowing with the normal document content.

What Other position Values Exist?

There are several important values:

  • static — the normal default positioning behavior.
  • relative — keeps the element in the normal layout but allows it to be offset and used as a reference for positioned children.
  • absolute — positions the element relative to a containing positioning context.
  • fixed — positions it relative to the viewport and keeps it attached to that viewport.
  • sticky — behaves normally until a scrolling threshold causes it to stick in a position.

We use fixed because our authentication overlay is intended to sit over the screen rather than behave like ordinary page content.

inset: 0

Next we have:

inset: 0;

At first this can look strange. What is inset?

inset is a shorthand property for the four directional offsets:

top
right
bottom
left

So:

inset: 0;

is roughly equivalent to:

top: 0;
right: 0;
bottom: 0;
left: 0;

Because our element is fixed to the viewport, placing all four edges at zero causes it to stretch across the available viewport.

Can inset Have Other Values?

Yes. You could write:

inset: 20px;

which gives all four sides a 20-pixel inset.

You can also specify different values:

inset: 10px 20px 30px 40px;

which follows the same top, right, bottom, left pattern used by other CSS shorthands.

display: flex

Now we reach one of the most important layout properties in modern CSS.

display: flex;

The display property tells the browser what kind of layout behavior an element should use.

The value flex activates Flexbox.

What Is Flexbox?

Flexbox is a CSS layout system designed to arrange elements in a row or column while making alignment and spacing easier to control.

We are using it because we have one main child — our Sign-In card — and we want to center that card.

What Other display Values Are Common?

You will eventually encounter values such as:

  • block — normal block layout.
  • inline — content flows within a line.
  • inline-block — behaves inline while still allowing box-like sizing.
  • flex — activates Flexbox.
  • grid — activates CSS Grid.
  • none — removes the element from the rendered layout.

align-items: center

Because we activated Flexbox, we can now use Flexbox alignment properties.

align-items: center;

align-items controls alignment along the Flexbox cross axis.

With the default horizontal flex direction, the cross axis is vertical, so center moves the card toward the vertical center.

What Other align-items Values Exist?

Common values include:

  • stretch — stretches items when possible.
  • flex-start — moves them toward the start of the cross axis.
  • flex-end — moves them toward the end.
  • center — centers them.
  • baseline — aligns text baselines.

justify-content: center

Now we need to center the card along the other axis.

justify-content: center;

justify-content controls how flex items are distributed along the main axis.

With the default flex direction, the main axis is horizontal. Therefore, center centers the card horizontally.

What Other justify-content Values Exist?

Some common values are:

  • flex-start
  • flex-end
  • center
  • space-between
  • space-around
  • space-evenly

These values determine how available space is distributed around or between the flex items.

padding: 20px

Finally, we add:

padding: 20px;

Padding is space inside the element, between its edge and its contents.

This matters because a very narrow screen could otherwise place the card directly against the edge of the viewport.

background: rgba(0,0,0,.7)

We also use a background color on the overlay, but this time the color is written using rgba().

rgba(0,0,0,.7)

rgb means red, green, and blue. The fourth value is alpha, which controls transparency.

The values mean:

red = 0
green = 0
blue = 0
alpha = .7

So this creates black with 70% opacity.

Unlike a fully opaque black background, the transparent black allows some of whatever is behind the overlay to remain visible.

What Could the Alpha Value Be?

The alpha channel ranges from 0 to 1.

rgba(0,0,0,0)
rgba(0,0,0,.5)
rgba(0,0,0,1)

0 means completely transparent, .5 means approximately half transparent, and 1 means completely opaque.

backdrop-filter: blur(8px)

Finally:

backdrop-filter: blur(8px);

backdrop-filter applies visual effects to the area behind the element.

blur(8px) tells the browser to blur that background by a radius of 8 pixels.

This is optional decoration rather than a requirement for centering the card. We use it because a subtle blurred background can make the authentication card feel separated from whatever is behind it.

Putting It All Together

.auth-overlay {
  position: fixed;
  inset: 0;
  display: flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  padding: 20px;
  background: rgba(0,0,0,.7);
  backdrop-filter: blur(8px);
}

Now the rule should no longer look like a collection of random properties. Each property has a job: position the overlay, make it cover the viewport, activate Flexbox, center the card, protect the edges, darken the background, and add a subtle blur.

Try It

Now build this complete rule in the editor. Then experiment with one property at a time. Change position: fixed to position: static and observe what changes. Try inset: 20px instead of 0. Change justify-content: center to flex-start. Change align-items: center to flex-start. Finally, experiment with the alpha value in rgba() and the blur value. Your goal is not just to make it work, but to understand what each property changes.

Contents.Title: CSS: Style the Card
Contents.Contents:
Design the Sign-In Card

Our overlay is now able to cover the screen and center its content. The next question is: what should the Sign-In card itself look like?

We already gave the card a class in HTML:

<section class="auth-card">
  ...
</section>

Because auth-card is a class, we select it with a dot:

.auth-card {

Now let's examine each property instead of treating this whole block as one mysterious decoration.

.auth-card {
  width: 100%;
  max-width: 400px;
  padding: 28px;
  background: #171a21;
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.1);
  border-radius: 16px;
  box-shadow: 0 20px 60px rgba(0,0,0,.45);
}

width: 100%

width controls the width of the element.

Here we write 100%.

A percentage is relative to the available size of the containing context.

So width: 100% tells the card to try to use all of the width available to it.

Could width Have Other Values?

Yes. You might write:

width: 300px;

which gives it a fixed width of 300 pixels.

You could also use other relative units.

Why use 100% here? Because we want the card to be able to shrink on smaller screens rather than always remaining at one fixed width.

max-width: 400px

Now you may ask: if the width is already 100%, why do we also need max-width?

Because 100% could become very wide on a large screen.

max-width places an upper limit on the width.

max-width: 400px;

This means the card can shrink below 400 pixels, but it should not become wider than 400 pixels.

This combination is extremely useful:

width: 100%;
max-width: 400px;

It basically means: use the available space when necessary, but never grow beyond a comfortable maximum size.

padding: 28px

Now let's think about the space inside the card.

padding creates space between the element's border and its content.

padding: 28px;

Every side receives 28 pixels.

You can also control the sides individually:

padding-top: 20px;
padding-right: 30px;
padding-bottom: 20px;
padding-left: 30px;

Or use shorthand:

padding: 20px 30px;

With two values, the first applies to top and bottom, while the second applies to left and right.

We use 28 pixels because the Sign-In card should have comfortable breathing room around the form.

background: #171a21

This gives the card its own surface color.

We use a slightly lighter dark color than the page background, which helps the card stand out.

Again, background can take many kinds of values, including named colors, hexadecimal colors, RGB colors, gradients, images, and more.

border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.1)

This single declaration contains several pieces of information.

border: width style color;

Our value is:

1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.1)

1px

This is the border width. It means the border should be one pixel thick.

solid

This is the border style.

Other border styles exist, such as dashed, dotted, double, and others.

rgba(255,255,255,.1)

This is the border color. Here we use white with only 10% opacity so the border is subtle rather than bright.

The result is a thin, faint edge around the card.

border-radius: 16px

border-radius controls how rounded the corners are.

border-radius: 16px;

A value of 0 would produce square corners.

A larger value creates rounder corners.

You can even use a very large percentage or pixel value to create pill-shaped or circular forms when the dimensions allow it.

box-shadow

Now for a property that beginners often see but do not understand immediately:

box-shadow: 0 20px 60px rgba(0,0,0,.45);

A common box-shadow pattern is:

horizontal-offset vertical-offset blur spread color

Our example is using an offset, a blur amount, and a color. The values create a soft shadow below and around the card.

What Does Each Number Mean?

The first 0 means there is no horizontal shift.

The 20px moves the shadow downward.

The 60px controls how soft and spread out the shadow appears through the blur.

The rgba() color controls how dark and transparent the shadow is.

Box shadows can have many combinations. You can make them small, large, sharp, soft, dark, colorful, or even use multiple shadows.

Why Are We Using a Shadow?

The shadow is not required for the card to function. It is a visual design choice that helps separate the card from the background and gives the interface a sense of depth.

Try It

Now reproduce the complete .auth-card rule in the editor. Then experiment with width, max-width, and padding to see how the card changes size. Change border-radius to 0, 30px, and a larger value. Change the border style from solid to dashed. Finally, change the box-shadow offsets and blur so you can see exactly which number changes which part of the shadow.

Contents.Title: CSS: Style the Heading and Subtitle
Contents.Contents:
Now Let's Design the Text Inside the Card

Our card exists, but the text inside it still uses the browser's default appearance. We now want the main heading to look like the title of an application and the supporting paragraph to look quieter.

First Selector: .auth-card h1

.auth-card h1 {
  margin: 0;
  text-align: center;
  font-size: 1.8rem;
}

This selector contains two parts: .auth-card and h1.

The space between them matters.

.auth-card h1 means: find an h1 that is inside an element with the auth-card class.

This is called a descendant selector.

Why Not Just Use h1?

You could write:

h1 {
  ...
}

but that would target every h1 on the page.

Our more specific selector allows us to say which h1 we actually mean.

margin: 0

Headings come with browser default margins. Here we remove that default outer spacing so we can control the layout ourselves.

As you learned earlier, margin is outside the element.

text-align: center

text-align controls the horizontal alignment of text within its container.

The value center centers the text.

Other common values include left, right, and justify.

font-size: 1.8rem

font-size controls how large the text appears.

Our value is 1.8rem.

rem is a relative unit based on the root element's font size.

Using relative units can make designs easier to scale than using only fixed pixels.

You could also write:

font-size: 24px;

or use other relative units.

Now Let's Handle the Paragraph

.auth-card p {
  text-align: center;
  color: #a9b0c0;
}

This selector means: find any paragraph inside the authentication card.

Again, the space means the paragraph is a descendant of the card.

Why Is the Subtitle a Different Color?

We want the user's eye to notice the main heading first. A softer text color makes the paragraph less visually dominant while keeping it readable.

What About Different Paragraphs?

If the Sign-In card eventually contains several paragraphs that should have different styles, we can create a class such as auth-subtitle and target that exact class instead.

This leads to an important CSS lesson: selectors should be as specific as necessary, but not more complicated than needed.

Try It

Now practice both selectors in the editor. Change text-align: center to left and then right to see how alignment changes. Change the heading's font-size from 1.8rem to 2.5rem and then to 1rem. Change the paragraph color to another color. Then try removing margin: 0 from the heading and observe the difference caused by the browser's default spacing.

Contents.Title: CSS: Style the Form Groups, Labels, and Inputs
Contents.Contents:
Now Make the Form Comfortable to Use

Our Sign-In card has the correct structure, but the fields need spacing and visual design. This lesson is especially important because several CSS concepts appear together.

First: Space the Form Groups

.form-group {
  margin-bottom: 15px;
}

We already learned that a class is reusable. Because every field group has the form-group class, this one rule can give every group the same bottom spacing.

margin-bottom controls the space outside the bottom edge of the element.

You could also write margin-top, margin-left, and margin-right, or use the shorthand margin.

Now Select the Labels

.form-group label {
  display: block;
  margin-bottom: 7px;
  font-size: .9rem;
  font-weight: 600;
}

.form-group label means: find a label that is inside an element with the form-group class.

display: block

The display property controls how the element participates in layout.

The value block makes the label behave like a block-level element, meaning it normally starts on its own line and can take up the available width.

Other common display values include inline, inline-block, flex, grid, and none.

margin-bottom: 7px

This places seven pixels of space below the label before the input begins.

If we changed it to 20px, the label and input would be farther apart.

font-size: .9rem

We slightly reduce the label size so it does not overpower the heading.

font-weight: 600

font-weight controls how thick or heavy the text appears.

Common numeric values include 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, and so on, depending on the font.

400 is commonly normal text, while 700 is commonly bold.

Here we use 600 to make the labels moderately strong without making them extremely bold.

Now Style the Input

.form-group input {
  width: 100%;
  padding: 12px 13px;
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.1);
  border-radius: 10px;
  outline: none;
  background: #1d2230;
  color: #e8eaf0;
  font: inherit;
}

width: 100%

The input should fill the available width of its containing form group.

This does not mean the input will always be 100 pixels wide. The percentage is relative to its containing space.

padding: 12px 13px

Here we use two values instead of one.

The first value, 12px, applies to the top and bottom.

The second value, 13px, applies to the left and right.

padding: 12px 13px;

is shorthand for:

padding-top: 12px;
padding-bottom: 12px;
padding-left: 13px;
padding-right: 13px;

border

We learned that borders have a width, style, and color.

border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,.1);

This makes a subtle one-pixel solid border around the input.

border-radius: 10px

Rounds the input's corners.

outline: none

Browsers normally draw a default outline around focused inputs. We are removing the browser's default outline because we will create our own focus appearance in the next lesson.

background

Gives the input its own dark surface, separating it from the slightly lighter card.

color

Sets the color of the text typed into the input.

font: inherit

This one can look unusual at first.

inherit tells the property to use the value inherited from the parent element instead of using an unrelated browser default.

Therefore font: inherit helps the input use the same font settings as the surrounding interface.

Why Did We Split the Styling Into Three Rules?

.form-group {
  ...
}

.form-group label {
  ...
}

.form-group input {
  ...
}

Each rule has a different responsibility:

The first controls the space around the field group.

The second controls the label.

The third controls the input itself.

Separating responsibilities makes a stylesheet easier to understand and change.

Try It

Now apply all three rules in the editor. Then change the form group's margin-bottom from 15px to 30px. Change the label's font-weight between 400 and 700. Change the input's padding values and observe how the input becomes taller or shorter. Change width: 100% to a smaller percentage and see how the field no longer fills the whole group. Finally, remove outline: none, focus the input, and compare the browser's default focus appearance with your custom styling.

Contents.Title: CSS: Show Focus
Contents.Contents:
Make the Active Input Visible

Imagine a user has two fields: Email and Password. They tap one of them and begin typing.

How should the interface communicate which field is currently active?

This is where the CSS :focus pseudo-class becomes useful.

.form-group input:focus {
  border-color: #6ea8fe;
  box-shadow: 0 0 0 3px rgba(110,168,254,.12);
}

What Is :focus?

:focus is a pseudo-class.

A pseudo-class describes a particular state of an element rather than selecting it only by its ordinary name or class.

For example, an input can exist normally, then become focused when the user clicks or taps it.

So:

.form-group input:focus

means: select inputs inside form groups while those inputs are focused.

border-color

We already have a border around the input. border-color changes only the border's color.

border-color: #6ea8fe;

So when the input is focused, the border becomes the accent color.

You can use any valid CSS color here, including hexadecimal, RGB, HSL, named colors, and more.

box-shadow

We also add a shadow around the input:

box-shadow: 0 0 0 3px rgba(110,168,254,.12);

This is not necessarily a large dramatic shadow. Here we are using it like a soft visual ring around the field.

Let's Read the Four Numbers

0 0 0 3px

The first value controls horizontal offset.

The second controls vertical offset.

The third controls blur.

The fourth controls spread.

Because the first three are zero, the shadow does not shift sideways, downward, or blur outward. The fourth value creates a 3-pixel ring around the input.

The last part is the semi-transparent accent color.

Why Not Just Change the Border?

We could simply change the border color. The additional box-shadow gives us a larger focus signal that is easier to notice.

Other Useful Pseudo-Classes

You will encounter other states such as:

  • :hover — while a pointer is over an element.
  • :active — while an element is being activated.
  • :focus — while an element is focused.
  • :disabled — when a control is disabled.
  • :checked — when certain controls are checked.

The important lesson is that CSS can style not only what an element is, but also what state that element is currently in.

Try It

Now add the focus rule to your project and click or tap each input. Change the accent color to another color. Change the border color and then change the shadow's spread from 3px to 6px. Remove the box-shadow and compare the difference. Then temporarily remove :focus from the selector and observe that the rule no longer waits for the input's focused state.

Contents.Title: CSS: Style the Login Button
Contents.Contents:
Make the Main Action Stand Out

The Login button is one of the most important elements on the screen. The user should be able to immediately recognize it as the primary action.

We first give the button a class:

<button class="auth-submit" type="submit">
  Login
</button>

Now CSS can select that specific class:

.auth-submit {
  width: 100%;
  padding: 12px;
  border: 0;
  border-radius: 10px;
  background: #6ea8fe;
  color: #07111f;
  font: inherit;
  font-weight: 700;
  cursor: pointer;
}

width: 100%

Just as we did with the input, the button can fill the available width.

padding: 12px

This gives the button internal breathing room, making the clickable area larger and more comfortable.

border: 0

Here we use a shorthand value of 0 instead of specifying a width, style, and color.

This means the button should have no visible border.

Why remove it? Because we want the background color and shape to define the main action visually.

border-radius: 10px

Rounds the button corners.

background: #6ea8fe

Creates the accent-colored button surface.

color: #07111f

Sets the text color. Notice that our button text is dark while the button background is light enough to keep the contrast readable.

font: inherit

Uses the surrounding font settings instead of a separate browser default.

font-weight: 700

Makes the text bold or strongly weighted. Remember that numeric weights are commonly interpreted with 400 around normal and 700 around bold, depending on the font.

cursor: pointer

This property controls the mouse pointer appearance when it is over the element.

cursor: pointer;

The pointer value typically gives the user a hand-shaped pointer, which communicates that the element is interactive.

There are many other cursor values, including default, not-allowed, text, grab, and others.

Now Add a Hover State

Our button can also react visually when the user points at it.

.auth-submit:hover {
  filter: brightness(1.08);
}

What Does :hover Mean?

:hover is another pseudo-class. It applies while the pointer is over the element.

What Is filter: brightness()?

The filter property can apply visual effects to an element. One available function is brightness().

filter: brightness(1.08);

A value of 1 represents the normal brightness. A value greater than 1 increases brightness, while a value below 1 reduces it.

For example:

filter: brightness(1.2);
filter: brightness(.8);

We use 1.08 for a subtle effect rather than an extreme change.

Try It

Now style the Login button exactly as shown. Then change width to 80% and observe the result. Change border-radius between 0, 10px, and 30px. Change the background color. Try different font-weight values. Change cursor: pointer to default. Finally, change the hover brightness to 1.2 and then .8 so you can see how the function changes the button.

Contents.Title: CSS: Design the Sign-Up Switch
Contents.Contents:
Style the Secondary Action

The Login action is the primary action, but the user also needs a way to move to the Sign-Up interface.

We can give the text area a class:

<p class="auth-switch">
  Don't have an account?
  <button type="button">Sign Up</button>
</p>

Now style the surrounding element:

.auth-switch {
  margin-top: 20px;
  color: #a9b0c0;
  text-align: center;
  font-size: .9rem;
}

margin-top

Unlike margin-bottom, this adds space above the element.

We use it to separate the Sign-Up switch from the form.

color

We use a muted color because the text is secondary information compared with the main Login action.

font-size

We use a slightly smaller size for the same reason.

Now Style the Button Inside It

.auth-switch button {
  border: 0;
  background: none;
  color: #6ea8fe;
  font: inherit;
  font-weight: 700;
  cursor: pointer;
}

This selector contains a class and a descendant element.

.auth-switch button means: find a button inside an element with the auth-switch class.

border: 0

Removes the button's visible border.

background: none

This removes the button's normal background so it can look like a text-based action rather than another large rectangular button.

color

The accent color makes the Sign Up action visually recognizable.

font: inherit

Makes the button use the surrounding font settings.

font-weight: 700

Makes the Sign Up text stronger than the surrounding sentence.

cursor: pointer

Provides a familiar pointer appearance when using a mouse or trackpad.

Why Make This Button Different From Login?

Design is also about hierarchy.

Login is the primary action, so it gets a filled accent-colored button. Sign Up is a secondary action, so it can look like a text link or lighter button.

This helps the user understand which action is the main one without needing to read every piece of text.

Try It

Now add the auth-switch styles and the auth-switch button styles to your editor. Change margin-top to different values and observe the spacing. Change the text color. Try giving the button a background color instead of none. Change the button's font weight and cursor. Then decide which combination makes the Sign-Up action look secondary while still being easy to discover.

Contents.Title: CSS: Create a Shared Theme
Contents.Contents:
Stop Repeating the Same Values

At this point you may have noticed that we keep typing the same colors again and again.

For example, the same dark background, panel colors, muted text, accent color, and border colors appear in different rules.

If you later decide that the blue accent should become purple, you would have to search through the whole stylesheet and change every copy.

CSS provides a better solution: custom properties, commonly called CSS variables.

:root {
  --bg: #0f1115;
  --panel: #171a21;
  --panel2: #1d2230;
  --text: #e8eaf0;
  --muted: #a9b0c0;
  --accent: #6ea8fe;
  --danger: #ff7f8a;
  --success: #72d6a0;
  --border: rgba(255,255,255,.1);
  --radius: 16px;
}

What Is :root?

:root is a pseudo-class selector that targets the document's root element. In a normal HTML page, that means the <html> element.

Placing our custom properties inside :root makes them easy to access throughout the stylesheet.

What Is --bg?

The two dashes at the beginning tell CSS that this is a custom property.

--bg: #0f1115;

The variable is called --bg, and its stored value is #0f1115.

You can create your own names. For example:

--main-color: blue;
--card-width: 400px;
--space-large: 30px;

The name itself has no magical meaning. We choose names that make the code understandable.

Using var()

Creating a variable is only half the process. We need to read its value.

body {
  background: var(--bg);
  color: var(--text);
}

var(--bg) tells CSS to use the value stored in --bg.

Why Is This Useful?

Imagine ten different rules all use var(--accent). If you change this:

--accent: #6ea8fe;

to:

--accent: #b48cff;

all of those rules can update to the new accent automatically.

The Variables We Created

--bg stores the main page background.

--panel stores the card or panel background.

--panel2 stores a second, slightly different surface color.

--text stores the main text color.

--muted stores less prominent text.

--accent stores the primary action color.

--danger stores a color for error or dangerous states.

--success stores a color for successful states.

--border stores the shared border color.

--radius stores the shared corner radius.

Can Variables Store Things Other Than Colors?

Yes. They can store lengths, font sizes, shadows, timing values, and many other CSS values.

--card-width: 400px;
--gap: 16px;
--main-font: system-ui, sans-serif;
--shadow: 0 20px 60px rgba(0,0,0,.45);

Try It

Now convert your repeated colors to CSS variables. Replace hard-coded values such as #0f1115 with var(--bg), panel colors with var(--panel), text colors with var(--text), muted colors with var(--muted), and your accent color with var(--accent). Then change the value stored in --accent and observe how multiple parts of your Sign-In design change together.

Contents.Title: CSS: Make the Sign-In Responsive
Contents.Contents:
Make the Interface Work on Different Screens

Our Sign-In card may look fine on a large screen, but what happens if the user opens the webpage on a narrow phone?

A good webpage should not assume that every device has the same amount of space.

Fortunately, some of our existing CSS already helps:

.auth-overlay {
  padding: 20px;
}

.auth-card {
  width: 100%;
  max-width: 400px;
}

Why Does width: 100% Help?

The card is allowed to use the available width of its parent. On a smaller device, that available width becomes smaller, so the card can shrink with it.

Why Does max-width: 400px Help?

On a large display, the card should not become enormous. The maximum width prevents that.

These two rules work together:

width: 100%;
max-width: 400px;

They mean: be responsive when space is limited, but remain comfortably sized when space is abundant.

Why Does padding: 20px Help?

Imagine a narrow phone. Even if the card can shrink, we still do not want it touching the very edge of the screen.

The overlay's 20-pixel padding reserves some space around it.

What About Even Smaller Screens?

Sometimes a design needs more than flexible widths. CSS also provides media queries, which allow us to apply different rules depending on the viewport size.

@media (max-width: 600px) {
  .auth-card {
    padding: 20px;
  }
}

What Does @media Mean?

A media query says: only apply the rules inside this block when the condition is true.

In this example:

max-width: 600px

means the rules apply when the viewport is 600 pixels wide or narrower.

Can Media Queries Use Other Conditions?

Yes. You can use conditions such as min-width, combine conditions, and target other features of the display.

For example:

@media (min-width: 1000px) {
  ...
}

applies the rules when the viewport is at least 1000 pixels wide.

Why Aren't We Rebuilding the Interface for Mobile?

Because responsive design usually means adapting the same interface rather than creating a completely separate webpage.

The same HTML can serve the desktop and mobile versions while CSS decides how much space each part receives.

Try It

Now test your responsive layout in the editor. Resize the preview area if your editor allows it. Change max-width: 400px to 300px and then to 500px. Change the overlay padding. Add the media query shown above and reduce the card padding when the viewport is 600 pixels or smaller. Your goal is to observe how the same HTML structure can adapt to different screen sizes without rebuilding it.

Contents.Title: CSS: Our Sign-In Design Is Finished
Contents.Contents:
Review the Design Layer

We started with a plain HTML structure and progressively added CSS. Now it is worth stopping and understanding what actually happened.

HTML Created the Structure

HTML gave us the elements that exist in the page:

  • containers
  • headings
  • paragraphs
  • forms
  • labels
  • inputs
  • buttons

HTML also gave certain elements additional information through attributes such as type, placeholder, required, for, id, and class.

CSS Created the Appearance

CSS changed the plain structure into a designed interface.

We used properties for:

  • spacing such as margin and padding
  • size such as width, max-width, min-height, and font-size
  • colors such as background and color
  • edges such as border and border-radius
  • positioning such as position, inset, and Flexbox properties
  • visual feedback such as :focus and :hover
  • responsive behavior through flexible widths and media queries

Why Did We Keep HTML and CSS Separate?

Because each technology has a different responsibility.

HTML
What exists?

CSS
How does it look?

JavaScript
What does it do?

This separation is one of the most important ideas to understand before moving into JavaScript.

We Did Not Add Classes Everywhere

We only introduced classes when we needed reusable targets for styling.

We Did Not Add IDs Everywhere

We introduced IDs when we needed a unique identity, such as connecting labels to inputs or preparing elements for JavaScript control.

Why Does That Matter?

Good HTML is not about filling every tag with as many attributes as possible. Good HTML is about using the right information for the right purpose.

Try It

Now go back through your editor and identify which parts of your project are HTML and which parts are CSS. Temporarily remove a CSS rule and observe what happens to the underlying HTML structure. Then restore the rule. Change a CSS value and observe how the structure stays the same while the appearance changes. This is the final reinforcement before we move from styling into JavaScript behavior.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Now We Add Behavior
Contents.Contents:
The Interface Looks Right — Now It Needs Behavior

At this point, our Sign-In interface can look like a real application, but it is still mostly static.

The HTML created the controls, and CSS changed how those controls look. Now we need something that can make the page respond when the user interacts with it.

This is where JavaScript becomes important.

What Will JavaScript Do?

JavaScript can respond to actions such as:

  • clicking a button
  • typing into an input
  • submitting a form
  • reading values from inputs
  • checking information entered by the user
  • changing text on the page

For our project, we are going to use JavaScript to create a very small learning version of authentication.

What Are We Building?

For now, we are not building a real account system with a server or database.

Instead, we will create a simple learning example with a fixed email and password written directly into the JavaScript code.

The idea is:

User types email and password
↓
JavaScript reads the values
↓
JavaScript compares them
↓
Correct → Login succeeds
Wrong → Login fails

This lets you learn the programming ideas behind authentication before introducing more advanced systems.

Later, this project can be expanded so that users can actually create accounts through a Sign-Up system. For now, we are focusing only on understanding how Login works.

Try It

Continue using the same project you have already built. Do not create a completely unrelated example. The goal is to make the Sign-In interface you already created become interactive.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: The Variable Basics
Contents.Contents:
Before We Add Functionality, We Need to Understand JavaScript

So far, we have built the structure of our Sign-In interface with HTML and designed it with CSS.

HTML tells the browser what exists.

CSS tells the browser how those things should look.

Now we are ready to introduce JavaScript.

Before we use the IDs from our HTML to make forms and buttons work, we first need to understand what JavaScript actually is and one of its most basic concepts: variables.

What Is JavaScript?

JavaScript is a programming language that allows a webpage to respond to actions and perform logic.

Without JavaScript, HTML and CSS can create a form that looks like a Sign-In page, but the page does not automatically know what should happen when the user submits that form.

JavaScript can make the webpage react.

For example, JavaScript can:

  • respond when a button is clicked
  • read values entered into inputs
  • check whether values meet certain conditions
  • show or hide elements
  • change text on the page
  • calculate values
  • store information temporarily while the program is running
  • communicate with a server

In our Sign-In project, JavaScript will eventually allow us to take the static interface we created and give it behavior.

Where Does JavaScript Go?

JavaScript can be written directly inside an HTML document using a <script> element.

<script>
  // JavaScript goes here
</script>

It can also be placed in a separate JavaScript file.

<script src="script.js"></script>

For this course, the important idea is that JavaScript is a separate layer from HTML and CSS.

HTML
What exists?

CSS
How does it look?

JavaScript
What does it do?

What Is a Variable?

A variable is a named place that JavaScript can use to hold a value.

For example:

const username = "Alex";

Here, username is the variable name and "Alex" is the value stored in it.

You can think of a variable as a labeled container.

username
↓
"Alex"

The label is username, and the value inside it is "Alex".

Later, JavaScript can use that value by referring to the variable name.

const username = "Alex";

console.log(username);

The browser's console would show:

Alex

This is one of the first important ideas in programming: instead of repeatedly writing a value, we can give it a name and use that name.

There Are Three Ways to Declare Variables

JavaScript provides three keywords that can be used to declare variables:

  • const
  • let
  • var

They all create variables, but they do not behave exactly the same way.

In modern JavaScript, you will normally use const and let. The older var keyword still exists and is important to understand because you will encounter it in older code and tutorials.

Using const

const is used when a variable should not be reassigned to a different value after it has been created.

const username = "Alex";

We can use the variable:

console.log(username);

But we cannot later do this:

username = "Jamie";

That attempts to give the username variable a completely new value.

Because it was declared with const, JavaScript does not allow that reassignment.

When Should We Use const?

Use const when you do not need to reassign the variable.

For example:

const email = "alex@example.com";
const password = "example123";

If the variable is only going to refer to that value during this part of the program, const is usually the appropriate choice.

Using let

let is used when a variable may need to be assigned a new value later.

let message = "Hello";

message = "Welcome";

At first, message contains "Hello".

Later, we assign "Welcome" to the same variable.

This is called reassignment.

let score = 0;

score = 10;
score = 20;

The variable remains score, but its value changes.

When Should We Use let?

Use let when you know the value needs to change while the program is running.

For example:

let loginAttempts = 0;

loginAttempts = loginAttempts + 1;

The number of login attempts can change, so let makes sense here.

Using var

var is another way to declare a variable.

var username = "Alex";

You may see var in older JavaScript programs, tutorials, or code written before modern JavaScript practices became common.

It can also be reassigned:

var username = "Alex";
username = "Jamie";

However, var has different scoping behavior from let and const.

For new JavaScript code, let and const are generally preferred because their behavior is easier to reason about in modern programs.

const vs let vs var

const
↓
The variable cannot be reassigned.

let
↓
The variable can be reassigned.

var
↓
Older variable declaration style with different scoping rules.

For most of the JavaScript we will write in this course, start by asking:

Does this variable need to be reassigned?

If the answer is no, use const.

If the answer is yes, use let.

You will learn more about the differences between these declarations as you continue learning JavaScript.

Variables Can Hold Different Types of Values

String

A string is text.

const username = "Alex";

The quotation marks indicate that Alex is text.

Number

A number does not need quotation marks.

const age = 18;

Because 18 is a number, JavaScript can perform mathematical operations with it.

Boolean

A boolean represents either true or false.

const loggedIn = false;

This type of value will become especially useful when we start writing conditions and authentication-like behavior.

Changing a Variable

When using let, we can change the value stored in the variable.

let status = "Logged out";

status = "Logged in";

The first line creates the variable.

The second line changes its value.

Notice that we do not write let again when reassigning it.

Displaying Information with console.log()

While learning JavaScript, we often need a simple way to see what our code is doing.

One useful tool is console.log().

const username = "Alex";

console.log(username);

console.log() sends a value or message to the browser's developer console.

We can also write a message directly:

console.log("Hello");

Or combine a message with a variable:

const username = "Alex";

console.log("Username:", username);

The console is extremely useful while learning because it lets us inspect values and see whether our JavaScript is behaving as expected.

A Login Example

Now we can use variables to represent information that might be involved in a Login process.

const email = "alex@example.com";
const password = "example123";

console.log("Email:", email);
console.log("Password:", password);

These variables are only examples for learning. We are not creating a real authentication system yet.

Temporary Values During a Program

Variables can also be used for temporary information while JavaScript is performing an operation.

const email = "alex@example.com";
const password = "example123";

console.log("Checking login...");
console.log(email);
console.log(password);

The variables hold the values that JavaScript needs at that moment.

Later, when we connect JavaScript to our HTML form, we can read what the user typed and place those values into variables.

Variables Are Not the Same as Authentication

This lesson is only teaching you how JavaScript stores and works with values.

We are not creating a real account system yet.

Later, we can use these JavaScript concepts to demonstrate basic authentication-like behavior using fixed example credentials. That will help you understand the programming logic before introducing a real backend and database.

What We Have Learned

  • JavaScript adds behavior and logic to webpages.
  • A variable gives a value a name so JavaScript can use it later.
  • const is normally used when a variable should not be reassigned.
  • let is used when a variable needs to be reassigned.
  • var is an older variable declaration style with different scoping behavior.
  • Variables can contain strings, numbers, booleans, and many other types of values.
  • console.log() can help us inspect values while learning and debugging.

Try It

Open your editor and create a few variables using const, let, and var. Give them different values such as text, numbers, and booleans. Use console.log() to display their values. Then create a let variable and reassign it to a different value. Finally, try changing a const variable and observe the error.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Add IDs for JavaScript Control
Contents.Contents:
Now We Have a Reason for More IDs

Earlier, we used IDs for connecting labels to inputs. JavaScript gives us another reason to use IDs: finding an exact element.

Our existing HTML already has these IDs:

id="email"
id="password"

We can use those exact IDs from JavaScript.

Give the Login Form an ID

Our original form does not have an ID yet. Now we need one because JavaScript needs to listen for its submission.

<form id="loginForm">
  ...
</form>

The form now has the unique ID loginForm.

The Email Input Already Has an ID

Earlier, we created:

<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" ...>

We do not need to create another ID for this input. JavaScript can use the existing email ID.

The Password Input Already Has an ID

<label for="password">Password</label>
<input id="password" type="password" ...>

Again, we can reuse the existing password ID.

Later We Will Add a Message Element

When we are ready to show the Login result directly on the page, we will add:

<div id="loginMessage"></div>

We are not adding it yet because we have not learned how JavaScript changes webpage content.

Why Are We Adding IDs?

We are not giving every HTML element an ID.

We only add or reuse an ID when JavaScript needs to identify a particular element.

That gives us a useful rule:

HTML element
↓
id="someName"
↓
JavaScript can find it

Try It

Add id="loginForm" to your existing Login form. Do not change the existing email and password IDs. We will use those exact IDs in the next lessons.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Find an Element
Contents.Contents:
Use getElementById()

Now that the Login form has an ID and the inputs already have IDs, JavaScript can find them.

The method we will use is getElementById().

const loginForm =
  document.getElementById("loginForm");

What Is document?

document represents the webpage currently loaded in the browser.

It gives JavaScript access to the HTML document.

What Does getElementById() Do?

getElementById() searches the webpage for an element with the ID we provide.

So this:

document.getElementById("loginForm")

means:

Find the HTML element whose ID is loginForm.

The Relationship Between HTML and JavaScript

HTML:
<form id="loginForm">

JavaScript:
document.getElementById("loginForm")

The same name connects the two layers.

Store the Result in a Variable

We normally store the element in a variable so we can use it later.

const loginForm =
  document.getElementById("loginForm");

Now loginForm refers to that HTML form.

Find the Existing Email Input

const emailInput =
  document.getElementById("email");

Notice that we are using the ID email, because that is the ID already used by our HTML.

Find the Existing Password Input

const passwordInput =
  document.getElementById("password");

Again, the JavaScript uses the exact ID that already exists in the HTML.

This is important because an ID is a connection between the HTML and JavaScript.

Try It

Practice finding loginForm, email, and password. The JavaScript names of the variables can be different, but the text inside getElementById() must match the HTML ID exactly.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Listen for the Login Form
Contents.Contents:
Wait for the User to Submit the Form

Finding the form is useful, but JavaScript still needs to know when the user is trying to log in.

That is where an event comes in.

What Is an Event?

An event is something that happens in the webpage.

Examples include:

  • click — a user clicks something.
  • input — the value of an input changes.
  • submit — a form is submitted.
  • focus — an element becomes focused.

For Login, the most useful event is submit.

Use addEventListener()

loginForm.addEventListener(
  "submit",
  function(event) {
    // Login code goes here
  }
);

addEventListener() tells JavaScript to wait for a specific event.

In our example, we are saying:

Watch the loginForm
↓
Wait for the submit event
↓
Run this function

What Is the Function Doing?

The function contains the instructions that should run when the event happens.

We do not need to run that function manually. The browser calls it when the form is submitted.

What Is event?

The event parameter represents information about the event that occurred.

We will use it to control the browser's normal form behavior.

Try It

Add the submit event listener to your Login form. For now, you can place a temporary console.log("Form submitted") inside the function to observe when the event runs. This is only a development tool; the actual Login result will later be shown on the webpage.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Prevent the Normal Form Submission
Contents.Contents:
Take Control of the Form

Normally, submitting an HTML form can cause the browser to perform its default form submission behavior.

For our learning project, we do not want the browser to immediately leave the page or reload it before our JavaScript can perform the Login check.

We can stop that default behavior.

loginForm.addEventListener(
  "submit",
  function(event) {
    event.preventDefault();
  }
);

What Does preventDefault() Mean?

preventDefault() tells the browser:

Do not perform the normal action for this event.

In our case, JavaScript wants to handle the Login process itself.

Why Is This Useful?

Without it, the browser's normal form behavior could happen before our JavaScript finishes the Login logic.

With it, we can safely continue:

Submit form
↓
Stop normal browser behavior
↓
Read email
↓
Read password
↓
Check credentials
↓
Show result

Important Idea

We are not preventing the user from submitting the form. We are preventing the browser's default behavior so that our JavaScript code can decide what should happen.

Try It

Add event.preventDefault() inside your submit listener. Submit the form and observe that the page stays where it is instead of following the browser's normal form submission behavior.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Read What the User Typed
Contents.Contents:
Getting the Email and Password

Now JavaScript can find the inputs and control the form submission. The next step is to actually read what the user typed.

An input's current text can be accessed through its value property.

Read the Email

const email =
  document.getElementById("email").value;

The browser looks for the input with the ID email, then reads its current value.

Read the Password

const password =
  document.getElementById("password").value;

Now we have two variables containing what the user entered.

const email = ...;
const password = ...;

What Is a Variable?

A variable gives us a name that refers to a value.

In this example, email refers to the email the user entered, while password refers to the password the user entered.

Why Store the Values?

We could repeatedly read the input values, but storing them in variables makes the code easier to understand.

Now our code can say:

if (email === ...) {
  ...
}

instead of repeatedly searching for the input.

Try It

Read both values and temporarily print them using console.log(). For example, use console.log(email) and console.log(password) while learning. Then type different values and watch the console change.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Create Fixed Login Credentials
Contents.Contents:
Our First Simple Authentication Check

We can now read what the user entered. But JavaScript still needs something to compare those values against.

This is where we create fixed credentials for our learning example.

Create a Fixed Email

const correctEmail = "student@example.com";

This variable stores the email address that our learning application expects.

Create a Fixed Password

const correctPassword = "1234";

This variable stores the password that our learning application expects.

We now have two different sets of values:

User input:
email
password

Expected values:
correctEmail
correctPassword

Why Use Variables?

We could write the text directly inside the comparison, but using variables makes the purpose much easier to understand.

const correctEmail = "student@example.com";
const correctPassword = "1234";

The variable names clearly tell us what the values represent.

Important: These Are Fixed Learning Credentials

These credentials are intentionally written directly in the JavaScript source code.

That is useful for learning because we can clearly see the authentication logic.

However, this is not how a real application should securely store passwords.

Later, when we study more advanced authentication, these fixed values can be replaced by a proper account system.

Try It

Create the two fixed credential variables in your JavaScript. You can change student@example.com and 1234 to other learning values and observe how the comparison changes later.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Compare the Login Information
Contents.Contents:
Now We Need to Compare the Values

We have everything needed for the basic authentication check:

  • the email entered by the user
  • the password entered by the user
  • the fixed email
  • the fixed password

Now we need to ask JavaScript whether they match.

The Strict Equality Operator

JavaScript uses === to check whether two values are equal in both value and type.

email === correctEmail

This asks:

Is the user's email exactly the same as the correct email?

We can do the same thing with the password:

password === correctPassword

We Need Both to Match

A Login should only succeed when both pieces of information are correct.

JavaScript can combine conditions with &&.

email === correctEmail &&
password === correctPassword

&& means and.

So the complete condition means:

The email must match AND the password must match.

What Happens When One Is Wrong?

Suppose the email is correct but the password is wrong.

email === correctEmail
true

password === correctPassword
false

Because both conditions are required, the overall result is false.

Try It

Practice comparing the user's values against the fixed credentials. Try changing one character in the email or password and observe whether the comparison becomes false.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Use if and else for Login Decisions
Contents.Contents:
Make JavaScript Decide Whether Login Succeeds

Knowing whether a condition is true or false is useful, but we need JavaScript to do something different depending on the result.

This is where if and else become important.

What Does if Mean?

if tells JavaScript:

Run this code only when this condition is true.

if (condition) {
  // code runs when condition is true
}

Add Our Login Condition

if (
  email === correctEmail &&
  password === correctPassword
) {
  // Login succeeded
}

Now JavaScript has a clear rule.

If both credentials match, it enters the code inside the braces.

What About Wrong Credentials?

We use else.

if (
  email === correctEmail &&
  password === correctPassword
) {
  // Login succeeded
} else {
  // Login failed
}

The else block runs when the if condition is false.

This Is the Core of Our Learning Authentication

User enters data
↓
JavaScript reads it
↓
JavaScript compares it
↓
if = correct credentials
↓
Login succeeds

else = incorrect credentials
↓
Login fails

Try It

Build the complete if and else structure in your editor. Do not worry about displaying a message yet. First make sure you understand how JavaScript chooses between the two branches.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Display the Login Result on the Page
Contents.Contents:
Tell the User What Happened

Now we have reached the point where our JavaScript needs to communicate with the person using the webpage.

The browser's developer console is useful while learning, but the actual Login result should appear directly on the webpage.

Create a Message Element

<div id="loginMessage"></div>

This gives us an empty area where JavaScript can place a message.

Find the Message Element

const loginMessage =
  document.getElementById("loginMessage");

We are using the same getElementById() idea that we already learned.

What Is textContent?

textContent allows JavaScript to change the text inside an HTML element.

loginMessage.textContent =
  "Login successful!";

The message element now displays:

Login successful!

Show a Failed Login

loginMessage.textContent =
  "Invalid email or password.";

The same element can display a different message depending on what happened.

Put It Into Our if and else

if (
  email === correctEmail &&
  password === correctPassword
) {
  loginMessage.textContent = "Login successful!";
} else {
  loginMessage.textContent =
    "Invalid email or password.";
}

Now the condition controls what the user sees.

Success

When both credentials match, JavaScript writes:

Login successful!

Failure

When either credential is wrong, JavaScript writes:

Invalid email or password.

Why Is This Better Than console.log()?

console.log() is primarily useful for developers while they are inspecting and debugging their code.

textContent changes the actual webpage, so the person using the application can see the result.

console.log()
↓
Developer sees it in the console

textContent
↓
User sees it on the webpage

Try It

Add the loginMessage element to your HTML and connect it to JavaScript. Test a correct Login and an incorrect Login. Notice how the visible message changes based on the authentication result.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Put the Login Logic Together
Contents.Contents:
Build the Complete Learning Login

We have now learned every individual part. It is time to combine them into one working Login process.

Here is the complete example using the exact IDs from our HTML:

const loginForm =
  document.getElementById("loginForm");

const loginMessage =
  document.getElementById("loginMessage");

const correctEmail = "student@example.com";
const correctPassword = "1234";

loginForm.addEventListener("submit", function(event) {

  event.preventDefault();

  const email =
    document.getElementById("email").value;

  const password =
    document.getElementById("password").value;

  if (
    email === correctEmail &&
    password === correctPassword
  ) {
    loginMessage.textContent = "Login successful!";
  } else {
    loginMessage.textContent =
      "Invalid email or password.";
  }
});

Let's Read It From Top to Bottom

First, JavaScript finds the Login form using the ID we added:

const loginForm =
document.getElementById("loginForm");

Then it finds the element that will display the result:

const loginMessage =
document.getElementById("loginMessage");

Next, we define the fixed credentials for our learning example:

const correctEmail = "student@example.com";
const correctPassword = "1234";

Then JavaScript waits for the form to be submitted:

loginForm.addEventListener("submit", function(event) {

We stop the browser's normal form behavior:

event.preventDefault();

Then we read the values from the existing HTML IDs:

const email =
document.getElementById("email").value;

const password =
document.getElementById("password").value;

Finally, we compare the entered values with the fixed credentials.

if (
  email === correctEmail &&
  password === correctPassword
)

Correct values produce a successful Login message. Incorrect values produce a failure message.

The Whole Idea

HTML
↓
Creates the Login form

CSS
↓
Makes the Login form look good

JavaScript
↓
Finds the elements
↓
Reads what the user enters
↓
Compares it with fixed credentials
↓
Makes a decision
↓
Shows the result

Try It

Build the complete example in your editor. Test the correct email and password first. Then change only the email. Then change only the password. Finally, change both. Observe how each test changes the result displayed on the page.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Understand What Authentication Means
Contents.Contents:
What Did We Actually Build?

We now have a very small authentication-like system.

The program takes information supplied by the user and compares it against information that the application already knows.

User provides credentials
↓
Application checks credentials
↓
Credentials match?
↓
Yes → Login succeeds
No → Login fails

What Is Authentication?

Authentication is the process of checking whether someone is the user they claim to be.

A Login form is one common place where authentication begins.

In our learning example, we are keeping the system intentionally simple:

correctEmail = "student@example.com"
correctPassword = "1234"

The program checks whether the entered values match those known values.

Why Is This Only a Learning Example?

The credentials are stored directly in JavaScript.

Anyone who can inspect the source code could potentially see them.

That means this is not secure authentication for a real application.

What Would a Real Application Need?

A real authentication system normally involves a server-side application, secure password handling, account storage, sessions or tokens, and other security measures.

We are intentionally not introducing all of that yet.

The goal at this stage is to understand the programming logic:

Receive input
↓
Compare values
↓
Make a decision
↓
Respond to the result

What About Sign Up?

A Login system assumes that an account already exists.

Creating that account is a different process called Sign Up or registration.

We are not building the account-creation system yet. It will make more sense after you understand how Login checks existing credentials.

Try It

Explain the Login process in your own words before continuing. You should be able to describe what the user enters, what JavaScript reads, what values are compared, what if does, what else does, and why the fixed credentials are only suitable for learning.

Contents.Title: JavaScript: Important Authentication Note
Contents.Contents:
This Is a Learning Authentication Demo

The Login system we created is intentionally simple so that the JavaScript logic is easy to understand.

Our fixed email and password are part of the JavaScript code:

const correctEmail = "student@example.com";
const correctPassword = "1234";

This is useful for practicing variables, comparisons, conditions, events, and DOM manipulation.

Do Not Treat This as Real Security

Never assume that putting an email and password inside browser JavaScript makes a real application secure.

The user can inspect client-side code, so secrets should not be protected this way.

A real authentication system needs a trusted server to perform important credential checks and other security operations.

Why Are We Learning It This Way?

Because programming concepts are easier to understand when we start with a small working example.

Right now, the important lesson is:

Input
↓
Variable
↓
Comparison
↓
Condition
↓
Result

Once these ideas make sense, more advanced authentication systems become much easier to understand.

Sign Up will be introduced later when the course is ready to move from checking an existing account to creating a new account.

Contents.Title: Final Checkpoint: Build the Sign-In Yourself
Contents.Contents:
Now Build the Login Yourself

You have now learned the basic structure, styling, and JavaScript behavior needed for a simple learning Sign-In system.

This checkpoint is different from simply copying the completed code. Your goal is to rebuild the process from the concepts you learned.

Build in This Order

  1. Create the HTML document.
  2. Create the main Sign-In container.
  3. Add the heading and supporting paragraph.
  4. Add the Login form.
  5. Add the email input with id="email".
  6. Add the password input with id="password".
  7. Use for and id when labels need to connect to inputs.
  8. Give the form id="loginForm" so JavaScript can find it.
  9. Add a Login button.
  10. Add a message element with id="loginMessage" for the result.
  11. Use getElementById() to find the elements.
  12. Use addEventListener() to listen for form submission.
  13. Use event.preventDefault() to control the form in JavaScript.
  14. Read the email and password using .value.
  15. Create fixed learning credentials using variables.
  16. Compare the entered credentials with ===.
  17. Use && when both credentials must match.
  18. Use if for successful authentication.
  19. Use else for failed authentication.
  20. Use textContent to display the result to the user.

The Goal Is Understanding

You are not expected to memorize every line of JavaScript.

You should be able to explain what each part is doing.

HTML
↓
Creates the Login interface

CSS
↓
Controls how it looks

JavaScript
↓
Finds the elements
↓
Reads the input
↓
Checks the credentials
↓
Makes a decision
↓
Shows the result

Things You Should Be Able to Explain

Why does the form have an ID?

Why does JavaScript use getElementById()?

Why does the email input use id="email"?

Why does the password input use id="password"?

Why do we use addEventListener()?

Why do we call event.preventDefault()?

What does .value give us?

What does === check?

What does && mean?

What is the difference between if and else?

What does textContent change?

Why are fixed credentials appropriate for this lesson but not for a real authentication system?

Final Practice

Rebuild the Login behavior in your editor without copying the complete example immediately.

Start by making the form work. Then read the inputs. Then create the fixed credentials. Then compare them. Finally, display the result.

When you are finished, test at least three cases:

  • Both credentials correct.
  • Correct email with the wrong password.
  • Wrong email with the correct password.

After this checkpoint, the next major step can be introducing how a user actually creates an account through Sign Up.

Try It

Rebuild the project from the concepts you learned. Only look back at the examples when you need help finding a mistake. The goal is not to reproduce the exact code from memory. The goal is to understand how the pieces connect and be able to build the process yourself.
